translationRepairs: The Grand Tutor and Grand Mentor stood south of Cross Street on the east side of the road, facing north with west at their right.
The Grand Tutor and Grand Commandant stood south of Cross Street on the east side of the road, facing north with west at their right.
Chinese 太師、太尉 pairs Grand Tutor with Grand Commandant; 太尉 is not Grand Mentor (太傅). The idiomatic replacement corrects the office title.
The Grand Tutor and Grand Mentor were also placed south of Cross Street, east of the road, facing north with west at their right.
The Grand Tutor and Grand Commandant were also placed south of Cross Street, east of the road, facing north with west at their right.
Chinese 太師、太尉 pairs Grand Tutor with Grand Commandant; 太尉 is not Grand Mentor (太傅). The literal replacement corrects the office title.
The Grand Tutor and Grand Mentor entered to their stations.
The Grand Tutor and Grand Commandant entered to their stations.
Chinese 太師、太尉入就位 names Grand Tutor and Grand Commandant; translating 太尉 as Grand Mentor confuses it with 太傅.
The Grand Tutor and Grand Mentor entered and took their places.
The Grand Tutor and Grand Commandant entered and took their places.
Chinese 太師、太尉入就位 names Grand Tutor and Grand Commandant; the literal's Grand Mentor misrenders 太尉.
The Grand Mentor washed at the lavabo below the east steps, entered the east chamber, brought the headband-and-comb box, knelt, and set it at the west end of the imperial seat.
The Grand Commandant washed at the lavabo below the east steps, entered the east chamber, brought the headband-and-comb box, knelt, and set it at the west end of the imperial seat.
Chinese subject is 太尉, the Grand Commandant; Grand Mentor would be 太傅. The idiomatic replacement restores the correct office.

The Grand Mentor went to the lavabo below the eastern steps, washed his hands, ascended by the east steps, went to the east chamber, took the headband-and-comb box forward, knelt, and set it at the west end of the imperial seat.

The Grand Commandant went to the lavabo below the eastern steps, washed his hands, ascended by the east steps, went to the east chamber, took the headband-and-comb box forward, knelt, and set it at the west end of the imperial seat.
Chinese subject is 太尉, the Grand Commandant; Grand Mentor would be 太傅. The literal replacement restores the correct office.
The Grand Mentor stepped forward left, knelt, removed the cap into the box, combed, set the headband, rose, stepped slightly west, and stood east-facing.
The Grand Commandant stepped forward left, knelt, removed the cap into the box, combed, set the headband, rose, stepped slightly west, and stood east-facing.
Chinese 太尉 is Grand Commandant, not Grand Mentor (太傅). The idiomatic replacement corrects the actor.
The Grand Mentor came forward slightly to the left, knelt, removed the cap and placed it in the box, combed the hair, set the headband, rose, moved slightly west, and stood facing east.
The Grand Commandant came forward slightly to the left, knelt, removed the cap and placed it in the box, combed the hair, set the headband, rose, moved slightly west, and stood facing east.
Chinese 太尉 is Grand Commandant, not Grand Mentor (太傅). The literal replacement corrects the actor.
The Grand Mentor stepped forward left, knelt, set the hairpin and tied the cap tassel, rose, and returned.
The Grand Commandant stepped forward left, knelt, set the hairpin and tied the cap tassel, rose, and returned.
Chinese 太尉 is Grand Commandant, not Grand Mentor (太傅). The idiomatic replacement corrects the actor.
The Grand Mentor came forward slightly left, knelt, set the hairpin, tied the cap tassel, rose, and returned to his place.
The Grand Commandant came forward slightly left, knelt, set the hairpin, tied the cap tassel, rose, and returned to his place.
Chinese 太尉 is Grand Commandant, not Grand Mentor (太傅). The literal replacement corrects the actor.
The Grand Mentor entered the outer east-wing curtain, washed, rinsed the goblet, poured ceremonial wine, covered it with ladle handle out, and stood inside facing south.
The Grand Commandant entered the outer east-wing curtain, washed, rinsed the goblet, poured ceremonial wine, covered it with ladle handle out, and stood inside facing south.
Chinese 太尉 is Grand Commandant, not Grand Mentor (太傅). The idiomatic replacement corrects the actor.

The Grand Mentor went within the curtain outside the wing, washed his hands, rinsed the goblet, poured the ceremonial wine, placed the ladle covering it with the handle outward, and stood within the wing facing south.

The Grand Commandant went within the curtain outside the wing, washed his hands, rinsed the goblet, poured the ceremonial wine, placed the ladle covering it with the handle outward, and stood within the wing facing south.
Chinese 太尉 is Grand Commandant, not Grand Mentor (太傅). The literal replacement corrects the actor.

The Grand Mentor presented one sliced bird; the emperor set the goblet west of the mat, took the stick, left on the base, right severed the tip to offer, tasted with the left hand, and gave it to the Grand Mentor.

The Grand Commandant presented one sliced bird; the emperor set the goblet west of the mat, took the stick, left on the base, right severed the tip to offer, tasted with the left hand, and gave it to the Grand Commandant.
Chinese twice names 太尉 as presenter and recipient; Grand Mentor would be 太傅. The idiomatic replacement corrects both occurrences.

The Grand Mentor took one sliced bird to present; the emperor set the goblet west of the offering mat, received the stick, extended left hand on the base, right severed the end to sacrifice, tasted with the left hand, and handed it to the Grand Mentor.

The Grand Commandant took one sliced bird to present; the emperor set the goblet west of the offering mat, received the stick, extended left hand on the base, right severed the end to sacrifice, tasted with the left hand, and handed it to the Grand Commandant.
Chinese twice names 太尉 as presenter and recipient; Grand Mentor would be 太傅. The literal replacement corrects both occurrences.
The Grand Mentor set it on the tray, descended, and stood south of the Grand Tutor.
The Grand Commandant set it on the tray, descended, and stood south of the Grand Tutor.
Chinese subject is 太尉 (Grand Commandant), distinct from 太師 (Grand Tutor) later in the same sentence; Grand Mentor misrenders 太尉.
The Grand Mentor placed it on the tray, descended, and stood south of the Grand Tutor.
The Grand Commandant placed it on the tray, descended, and stood south of the Grand Tutor.
Chinese subject is 太尉 (Grand Commandant), distinct from 太師 (Grand Tutor) later in the same sentence; Grand Mentor misrenders 太尉.
The Grand Tutor and Grand Mentor returned south of Cross Street.
The Grand Tutor and Grand Commandant returned south of Cross Street.
Chinese 太師、太尉复横街南位 pairs Grand Tutor with Grand Commandant; Grand Mentor is 太傅, not 太尉.
The Grand Tutor and Grand Mentor returned to their places south of Cross Street.
The Grand Tutor and Grand Commandant returned to their places south of Cross Street.
Chinese 太師、太尉复横街南位 pairs Grand Tutor with Grand Commandant; Grand Mentor is 太傅, not 太尉.
The Grand Tutor and Grand Mentor left.
The Grand Tutor and Grand Commandant left.
Chinese 太師、太尉出 names Grand Tutor and Grand Commandant; translating 太尉 as Grand Mentor confuses it with 太傅.
The Grand Tutor and Grand Mentor departed.
The Grand Tutor and Grand Commandant departed.
Chinese 太師、太尉出 names Grand Tutor and Grand Commandant; the literal's Grand Mentor misrenders 太尉.
The edict ran: "By edict: Crown Prince So-and-so, on this auspicious day receives the cap of adulthood per ancient statute; Grand Mentor So-and-so is ordered to the palace to perform the rite."
The edict ran: "By edict: Crown Prince So-and-so, on this auspicious day receives the cap of adulthood per ancient statute; Grand Commandant So-and-so is ordered to the palace to perform the rite."
Chinese edict appoints 太尉某, the Grand Commandant; Grand Mentor would be 太傅. The idiomatic replacement restores the office named in the edict.

The edict was proclaimed: "By edict: the crown prince So-and-so, on this auspicious day receives the additional cap of adulthood; follow the old statutes; we appoint Grand Mentor So-and-so to go to the palace and perform the rite."

The edict was proclaimed: "By edict: the crown prince So-and-so, on this auspicious day receives the additional cap of adulthood; follow the old statutes; we appoint Grand Commandant So-and-so to go to the palace and perform the rite."
Chinese edict appoints 太尉某, the Grand Commandant; Grand Mentor would be 太傅. The literal replacement restores the office named in the edict.
The crowner knelt and set the cup east of the offering mat, rose, and stood south-facing west of the seat.
The capped prince ascended the mat, knelt and set the cup east of the offering mat, rose, and stood south-facing west of the seat.
In the capping sequence, 冠者 is the newly capped prince (after 皇子…降筵 and 賓答拜), not the crowning guest; the idiomatic also restores omitted 升筵.
The crowner ascended the mat, knelt and set the cup east of the offering mat, rose, and stood west of the mat facing south.
The one who was capped ascended the mat, knelt and set the cup east of the offering mat, rose, and stood west of the mat facing south.
Chinese 冠者升筵 continues the capped prince's wine rite after the guest's answering bow; crowner wrongly treats 冠者 as the guest who crowns.
The cap-assistant knelt and removed the advancement-worthy cap; the guest stepped down three ranks, took the coronet, and crowned him.
The guest's cap-assistant knelt and removed the advancement-worthy cap; the guest stepped down three ranks, took the coronet, and crowned him.
Chinese 賓之贊冠者 explicitly attributes the cap-assistant to the guest; the idiomatic had dropped that 賓之 attribution present in the source.
The prince rose; the guest bowed to the prince to go to the inner room; dressed in dragon robes and came out square west of the inner room door facing south.
The prince rose; the guest bowed to the prince to go to the inner room; he dressed in dragon robes and came out west of the inner room door facing south.

Chapter 出方房戶西 is a variant; Wikisource Xin Tang shu juan 17 has the parallel 出房戶西 (as in nearby units), so 方 is not 'square', and the literal correctly drops that misreading while restoring the subject.
When the guest left, the prince received him east-facing; kinsmen bowed; the prince returned the bow.
When the guest left, the prince appeared east-facing; the kinsmen bowed to him; the prince returned the bow.
Chinese 皇子東面見，諸親拜之 has the prince appear east-facing so that the kinsmen bow to him after the guest departs; he does not receive the departing guest.
At first, when the guest departed, the prince received him facing east; kinsmen bowed to him; the prince returned the bow.
At first, when the guest departed, the prince appeared facing east; the kinsmen bowed to him; the prince returned the bow.
Chinese 見 here is the prince presenting himself for the kinsmen's salute (諸親拜之), not receiving the guest who has already left (賓出).
The guest filled the courtyard, bowed east, and left; grooms followed; followers received the horses with obeisance outside the gate.
The guest, facing the courtyard gifts, bowed east and left; grooms followed; followers received the horses with obeisance outside the gate.
Chinese 賓當庭實 is positional—facing the courtyard gifts (庭實)—not that the guest filled the courtyard; the idiomatic replacement restores that sense.
The guest filled the courtyard, bowed east, departed; horse-leaders followed out; followers received the horses with obeisance outside the gate.
The guest, facing the courtyard gifts, bowed east and departed; horse-leaders followed out; followers received the horses with obeisance outside the gate.
Chinese 當庭實 marks position relative to the courtyard gifts, not filling the courtyard; the literal replacement restores that positional sense.
the third: first-rank sons dragon robes; second startled; third fine-fur; fourth fine-silk; fifth black; sixth through ninth cap and coronet.
the third: first-rank sons dragon robes; second pheasant; third fine-fur; fourth fine-silk; fifth black; sixth through ninth cap and coronet.
In the ranked coronet sequence, chapter 驚冕 corresponds to Wikisource 鷩冕 (pheasant coronet) for second-rank sons; translating 驚 as 'startled' misreads the dress grade.

the third crowning: first-rank sons use dragon robes, second-rank sons startled robes, third-rank sons fine-fur robes, fourth-rank sons fine-silk robes, fifth-rank sons black robes, sixth through ninth-rank sons use cap and coronet.

the third crowning: first-rank sons use dragon robes, second-rank sons pheasant robes, third-rank sons fine-fur robes, fourth-rank sons fine-silk robes, fifth-rank sons black robes, sixth through ninth-rank sons use cap and coronet.
